t: Count Numbers with Unique Digits — Combinatorial Counting
o: We must count all integers x with 0 <= x < 10^n whose decimal digits are all distinct. For n = 2, the range is [0, 100): the 10 single-digit numbers plus the two-digit numbers with distinct digits — 9 choices for the first digit (1-9) and 9 for the second (0-9 minus the first) = 81, giving 91 total. For n = 0, only x = 0 qualifies, so the answer is 1. Since n <= 8, any number in range has at most 8 digits, and a number with more than 10 digits could never have all unique digits anyway. This tiny bound means we can either enumerate smartly or, better, count directly with a simple product formula per digit-length.
k: A k-digit number (no leading zero) has 9 * 9 * 8 * ... distinct-digit arrangements: 9 choices for the first digit, then one fewer choice each step.
The answer is cumulative: f(n) = f(n-1) + (count of exactly-n-digit numbers with unique digits).
Since n <= 8, an O(n) closed-form loop is trivially fast; brute force over 10^n numbers is also feasible but wasteful.

a.i: Simply iterate every integer from 0 to 10^n - 1 and check whether its digits are distinct using a boolean array of size 10. With n <= 8 this checks at most 100 million numbers, which is borderline but acceptable given the constraint; it is the most direct translation of the problem statement.
s: For each x from 0 to 10^n - 1, extract its digits.
Use a seen[10] boolean array; if any digit repeats, skip the number.
a.t: O(10^n * d) where d <= n is the digit count of each checked number — up to ~10^8 operations at n = 8.
a.sp: O(d) extra space for the digit-checking buffer/array.

a.i: Count numbers by their exact length and sum. There is 1 valid number with 0 digits (just 0). A k-digit number with unique digits: 9 choices for the leading digit (1-9), then 9 choices for the next (any of 10 except the first), then 8, and so on — i.e., 9 * P(9, k-1). So f(n) = 1 + sum_{k=1..n} 9 * 9!/(10-k)! computed iteratively by multiplying a running product by (11 - k) each step.
s: Handle n = 0 by returning 1 immediately (or via initialization).
Set ans = 1 (counts x = 0) and cur = 9 (count of length-1 numbers).
For k from 2 to n: multiply cur by (11 - k) to get the count of k-digit numbers with unique digits.
Add cur to ans after each multiplication.
a.t: O(n) — a single loop of at most 8 iterations computing the running product.

w: In an interview, mention brute force briefly, then present the combinatorial counting approach as the intended solution — it runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. Key pitfalls: forgetting that n = 0 returns 1 (only x = 0), miscounting the first digit (it cannot be 0, hence 9 choices, not 10), and off-by-one errors in the multiplier sequence 9, 9, 8, 7, ... (implemented as multiplying by 11 - k at step k). Edge cases: n = 0 -> 1, n = 1 -> 10, n = 8 -> 2345851. Likely follow-ups: extend to counting unique-digit numbers in an arbitrary range [L, R] (requires digit DP), or handle n larger than 10 (answer saturates since no number can have more than 10 unique digits).
